The director and her cast scope out the emotional truths in the piece.

It’s worth remembering that it was only after the armistice that some British women over 30 got the right to vote, and that Coward, the wannabe playwright, had been working as a child actor and then a juvenile since 1911.
This remains a thought-provoking piece, raising interesting points about the ways in which couples can drift into stifling gender roles.
Troupe make a staunch case for Coward's youthful effort.

It feels like a case of an earnest 18-year-old writer (Coward) wishing he was more like the mighty Norwegian dramatist Henrik Ibsen: not just witty, but deep, too. The persistently shelved 1918 drama, from which Coward later distanced himself, has been bravely abridged by Bill Rosenfield.
Ward’s production takes the play seriously as social commentary with feminist messaging, and it could even be considered a tragedy.
What emerges is a sensitive, stylish revival that highlights Coward’s early preoccupation with love and the fragile architecture of marriage.
A strong cast and an engaging, still-timely plot make this a joy for any Coward fan.
Overall a compelling case has been made for the play’s reintroduction to the canon.
Even so, the Troupe company delivers an entertaining evening, in the same vein as their two-part The Forsyte Saga, previously staged at the same address and then transferred to the RSC.
Rosenfield’s reimagining largely lands in trimming the play’s fat and enabling Sheila’s desperation to come to the fore.
The characters, the dialogue and the storyline are believable and entertaining.

cn.t: Coward's rarely-seen debut, written at 18, proves surprisingly timeless in its portrait of marriage stifling a female writer. Critics find it darker and more Ibsen than typical Coward, with most praising the sharp reimagining despite some pacing issues.
